source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures: a theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test (as described in Little et al. 2014)
finding: Items are solved by finding correspondences between cells, then applying rules from a small taxonomy: constant in a row, pairwise progression (increment or decrement), figure addition or subtraction (OR/AND type), distribution of three, distribution of two (XOR type).
numbers: Number of rule tokens in a problem explained 57% of the variance in item accuracy. Distribution-of-2 (XOR) items appear only late in the test, where accuracy is lowest.
limits: Primary text not opened (403 on DTIC and CMU). Numbers come from Little et al. 2014, a secondary source.
agent_relevance: A rule taxonomy plus a count of rule tokens predicts difficulty. The S0 gate can use rule type and token count as a difficulty estimate before choosing how much budget to spend.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures: a theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test (as described in Little et al. 2014)
finding: Two production-system models were built. FAIRAVEN had no strategic memory organisation and no access to the distribution-of-2 rule; it matched median Raven performers. BETTERAVEN had better control processes and all rule types; it matched the very best performers.
numbers: Models were consistent with accuracy, response time and eye-fixation data. Sample sizes and fixation statistics not read this session.
limits: Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Ability differences were modelled as goal management and rule access, not as new knowledge. This supports a code-held goal stack (the program keeps the goals) rather than asking the model to remember them.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures: a theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test (as described in Little et al. 2014)
finding: The models worked in four steps: find correspondences between symbolic features of cells, move them to a working-memory buffer where matching rules fire, use the rules to generate the missing cell, then search the answer options for the best match.
numbers: No numbers. This is constructive matching: build the answer first, then look at the options.
limits: Secondary description. The step list is Little et al.'s paraphrase.
agent_relevance: Maps onto a scaffold order: induce the rule from the given cells, generate the expected answer, only then compare with candidates. Avoid option-first guessing.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better
finding: Earlier studies (Wiley 2011, Salthouse 1993, Unsworth and Engle 2005) found that the working-memory correlation did NOT rise with item difficulty, which was taken as a refutation of Carpenter et al. Little et al. show the flat pattern appears only when the overall correlation is low.
numbers: Simulation slopes of item-wise correlation vs item position: 0.0002, 0.0006, 0.0009, 0.0013, 0.0015, 0.0016 for overall rho = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9.
limits: Simulation depends on assumptions (bivariate normal scores, fixed item accuracies). Floor effects give an inverted U at very high rho.
agent_relevance: A prediction of the founding theory looked refuted but was a measurement artefact. Do not drop a mechanism (goal holding) on one null result from a weak measure.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better
finding: Behavioural study with a four-task composite working-memory score and the Advanced Matrices (Set II, 36 items). The composite gave a higher overall correlation with the test, and the item-wise correlation rose with item difficulty.
numbers: N = 126 after exclusions. Overall r(composite WMC, RAPM) = 0.56. Slope of item-wise point-biserial correlation 0.004, t(34) = 2.87, p < .01, r2 = 0.20. Operation span alone: overall r = 0.36 and no significant slope.
limits: One sample, one test version. A second study is in the supplement and was not read.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that harder items load more on holding and combining rules. Hard items are where offloading memory to code should pay most.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better
finding: Two rival accounts from Wiley et al. 2011 did not hold up here: novel rule combinations did not raise the working-memory link, and rule-token count was tested separately.
numbers: Novelty effect in the multilevel model not significant (p = 0.39). Wiley et al. 2011 had reported token-wise correlations r = 0.25, 0.24, 0.33, 0.21 for items with 1, 2, 3, 4 tokens (flat).
limits: Novel items were defined by Wiley's list (items 2, 10, 14, 16, 18, 21, 25, 28, 30, 31, 35).
agent_relevance: The role of rule novelty is not settled. Do not build a gate on 'novel rule means more effort' without testing it.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better
finding: Easy Raven items are solved by more than 90% of people and the hardest by fewer than 10%. Accuracy falls with item position by design.
numbers: Descriptive: over 90% on early items, under 10% on the last items of the Advanced test.
limits: Population figures quoted in the paper's introduction, not new data.
agent_relevance: Difficulty is graded within one test. Use graded item pools when we test the S0 gate, so easy and hard items are both present.

source: Zhang, Gao, Jia, Zhu, Zhu (2019) RAVEN: a dataset for relational and analogical visual reasoning
finding: Procedurally generated Raven-style problems built from an image grammar. Rules follow Carpenter et al.: Constant, Progression, Arithmetic, Distribute Three (Distribute Two merged into Three). 8 rule instantiations, 4 structures, 7 figure configurations, 1,120,000 structure annotations.
numbers: Humans (college students) 84.41% mean. Symbolic heuristic solver with rule access: perfect. Best vision model ResNet+DRT 59.56%. LSTM 13.07%, WReN 14.69%, CNN 36.97%, ResNet 53.43% (chance 12.5%).
limits: Human test was on a subset of 'easily perceptible' examples only. The answer set is made by changing one attribute, which later work showed leaks the answer (see the I-RAVEN line).
agent_relevance: Once cells are symbols, Raven is a search problem a program solves exactly. The hard part is perception. A scaffold should turn the problem into symbols and let code do the rule search.

source: Zhang et al. (2019) RAVEN
finding: Auxiliary rule-classification training hurt rather than helped on RAVEN, unlike the claim in Barrett et al. 2018.
numbers: ResNet+DRT 59.56% down to 20.71% with a rule-classification loss; 59.56% down to 56.86% with a structure loss. WReN 14.69% down to 12.58% with a structure loss.
limits: One architecture family and one dataset.
agent_relevance: Extra rule-label supervision is not a free gain. Rule labels in a prompt may likewise not help; test it.

source: Zhang et al. (2019) RAVEN
finding: WReN, strong on Barrett's dataset, was near chance on RAVEN, and did better on grid-like layouts than on layouts with independent components. A plain CNN doubled WReN.
numbers: WReN 14.69% overall vs CNN 36.97% and ResNet 53.43%. Human-model gap up to 37 points on 2x2Grid.
limits: Failure to replicate a model result on a new dataset; the authors blame layout diversity.
agent_relevance: Results on one generated test do not transfer. Judge any scaffold gain on several layouts of the same task.

source: Barrett, Hill, Santoro, Morcos, Lillicrap (2018) Measuring abstract reasoning in neural networks
finding: PGM dataset of Raven-like matrices (relation, object, attribute triples) with controlled generalisation regimes. The relational WReN model was best on the neutral split.
numbers: Neutral split test accuracy: WReN 62.6%, Wild-ResNet 48.0%, ResNet-50 42.0%, LSTM 35.8%, CNN+MLP 33.0%, context-blind ResNet 22.4% (chance 12.5%). Without distractor attribute values WReN reaches 78.3% test. Auxiliary symbolic-target training gave +13.9 points on the neutral split.
limits: No human baseline by design. A context-blind model scoring 22.4% shows answer-set shortcuts exist.
agent_relevance: Answer options alone carry signal. An agent that reads options first can be fooled; code should hide options during rule induction (matches the spirit of G3).

source: Barrett et al. (2018)
finding: Generalisation was uneven: held-out combinations of familiar triples transferred better than new attribute values, and the model was weaker at extrapolation. The model was more accurate when more certain of its predicted symbolic rules.
numbers: Interpolation was the least problematic regime (generalisation error 14.6%). Certainty of meta-target prediction tracked answer accuracy (figure, no single number read).
limits: Appendix breakdowns only skimmed.
agent_relevance: A model's own rule prediction can serve as a confidence signal, if code checks it.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 was given Digit Matrices, a new text-only task modelled on Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices, with constant, distribution-of-3, progression and logic (OR, AND, XOR) rules. Zero-shot, no examples. It beat the human average.
numbers: Humans N = 40 UCLA undergraduates (3 more excluded). GPT-3 vs humans, generative answers: OR = 1.88, p = 0.005; multiple choice: OR = 6.27, p = 2.3e-8. The best human answered every problem correctly.
limits: Text digits, not visual input. GPT-3 era model. Later work (not read here) questions how robust the result is.
agent_relevance: Text-form matrix rules are within reach of a language model. Converting a visual item into digits or symbols may be the key step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023)
finding: GPT-3 showed the same difficulty effects as humans: progression rules harder than non-progression, more unique rules harder, permuted logic items harder than aligned ones.
numbers: Item-type profile correlation GPT-3 vs humans r(30) = 0.39, p = 0.027. Progression vs none: humans OR = 0.41, GPT-3 OR = 0.07. Number of unique rules: humans OR = 0.61, GPT-3 OR = 0.25. Spatial alignment in logic items: humans OR = 0.52, GPT-3 OR = 0.06.
limits: Correlation is modest. GPT-3 effects are larger than human effects on all three, so it is more fragile.
agent_relevance: The same difficulty drivers (rule type, number of distinct rules, layout) apply to a language model. Use them as S0 difficulty features.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023)
finding: Beyond matrices, GPT-3 matched or beat students on letter-string and verbal analogies but lost to students on picking the analogous story by higher-order relations.
numbers: Letter strings: N = 57 students, GPT-3 vs humans OR = 1.76, p = 6.3e-5, mostly on zero-generalisation items. Story analogies N = 54: humans better, OR = 0.37, p = 0.0003; 15 of 54 humans chose the analogous story on every trial.
limits: Same model and lab throughout; no later-model replication read here.
agent_relevance: Strong on tight symbolic rules, weaker on loose relational similarity between rich texts.

source: Gendron, Bao, Witbrock, Dobbie (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Eight LLMs on text versions of RAVEN (RAVEN-T, in natural-language text and symbolic form, multiple choice and open answer), plus ARC, ACRE and others. Performance was poor except for the strongest models; giving answer choices helped.
numbers: Open-ended RAVEN-T text/symbolic: GPT-4 41.0%/33.0%, Text-Davinci-3 34.3%/23.4%, GPT-3.5-Turbo 22.6%/16.1%, Zephyr-7B 0.9%/14.5%. Multiple choice text/symbolic: GPT-4 69.7%/53.5%, Davinci-3 46.1%/45.2%, GPT-3.5 27.6%/31.5%; chance 12.5%.
limits: Many open models fall below chance when they give no valid answer. Raven is probably in the training data (the authors checked that the models describe it).
agent_relevance: Option sets give large lifts (GPT-4 33% to 53% symbolic). Do not credit the agent with rule induction when options leaked the answer.

source: Gendron et al. (2023)
finding: Chain-of-thought did not help overall, and fine-tuning LLaMA2 on RAVEN-T gave near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but a clear drop on compositional out-of-distribution splits (four figures, nested figures).
numbers: Fine-tuned LLaMA2 close to perfect on the RAVEN-T test split; accuracy dropped sharply on the -Four and -In-Center splits (exact values in Table 6, not recorded). CoT results in the appendix not above base models overall.
limits: Compositional splits built by the authors; only LLaMA2 was fine-tuned.
agent_relevance: Training on rule patterns teaches syntax, not abstraction. A scaffold must not rely on memorised patterns.

source: Zhang, Jia, Zhu, Zhu (2021) Abstract spatial-temporal reasoning via probabilistic abduction and execution (PrAE)
finding: Neuro-symbolic model: neural perception gives probabilistic attributes, a symbolic engine abduces the rules (Carpenter-style taxonomy) and executes them to generate the answer. It beats monolithic networks and beats humans on three configurations.
numbers: RAVEN / I-RAVEN mean accuracy, trained on 2x2Grid only: PrAE 65.03 / 77.02; CoPINet 52.96 / 22.84; SRAN 15.56 / 29.06; ResNet+DRT 31.56 / 13.26; WReN 9.86 / 14.87; humans 84.41 on RAVEN.
limits: Fails on 3x3Grid and on overlapping layouts (marginalising over many objects accumulates error). I-RAVEN is the answer-set-balanced version by Hu et al.
agent_relevance: Perception first, rules by code, answer by generation: the same split our scaffold uses (model reads, program reasons).

source: Zhang et al. (2021) PrAE
finding: When the shortcut in the original answer set is removed (I-RAVEN), models that looked strong drop a lot, while the symbolic model does not. Original RAVEN scores partly measured answer-set bias.
numbers: CoPINet 52.96 on RAVEN down to 22.84 on I-RAVEN; PrAE 65.03 up to 77.02. A context-blind ResNet in Barrett et al. reached 22.4% without seeing the matrix.
limits: I-RAVEN itself is from Hu et al., cited in the paper and not read.
agent_relevance: Check any Raven result for option-set leaks. Run a context-blind control on our own tests.

source: Ahrabian et al. (2024) The curious case of nonverbal abstract reasoning with multi-modal large language models
finding: Open and closed multimodal models on IQ50 (50 human-made puzzles), RAVEN-S (3,500 sampled items) and CCSE. No model reliably beat the random baseline across all three datasets zero-shot.
numbers: Models within -8.7 to +7.3 points of random on IQ50, -1.0 to +0.6 on RAVEN-S, -5.6 to +6.4 on CCSE. IQ50 humans: 25 participants, 95.9% (SD 6.92). Best accuracy within 2% of the majority baseline.
limits: 2023-era models (GPT-4V, Gemini Pro Vision, LLaVA, Qwen-VL). Newer models not covered.
agent_relevance: Matching the majority answer can fake skill. Always compare to majority and random controls.

source: Ahrabian et al. (2024)
finding: Reasoning and answers disagreed. A corrective hint after a wrong first try helped; general and sample-specific hints hurt. Chain-of-thought demonstrations boosted GPT-4V a lot.
numbers: Joint answer plus reasoning correct: GPT-4V 26%, best open model 4% (open average 1%). Faithfulness of reasoning to answer: 50% GPT-4V, 25% Gemini Pro Vision. Corrective hints or CoT few-shot raised GPT-4V by up to 100% (relative). Safeguard refusals rose from 4% to 18% with one-shot.
limits: Relative gains from a low base. Hints written by authors who knew the answer.
agent_relevance: Fits G2: revision works when it uses real feedback on the output, not generic hints. Also, reasoning text is often unfaithful to the answer.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) MARVEL: multidimensional abstraction and reasoning through visual evaluation and learning
finding: 770 abstract visual puzzles across six core-knowledge patterns and five layouts (including Raven-type matrices), each with perception questions. All models were near random.
numbers: Humans (30 annotators, ages 10 to 50) 68.86% (SD 9.74). Closed-source MLLMs average 25.7%, open-source 24.0%, a gap of about 40 points. Best perception-plus-answer consistency only 5.97%.
limits: Puzzle set built by the authors; humans solved a subset.
agent_relevance: Perception errors are the bottleneck. Adding text descriptions of panels lifted closed models, so describe first, then reason.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: On ConceptARC (480 tasks, 16 concepts) text-only GPT-4 was far below humans, and the visual GPT-4V did far worse than text on the simplest tasks.
numbers: Humans 91%; Kaggle winner 52%; GPT-4 33% (temperature 0 and 0.5, one-shot prompt). Minimal tasks (48): humans 95%, GPT-4 69% (temp 0) and 65% (temp 0.5), GPT-4V 25% zero-shot and 23% one-shot. 12 of 482 humans excluded for failing minimal tasks.
limits: ConceptARC is grid transformation, not Raven; included as the nearest abstraction benchmark. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Vision input collapses accuracy even on minimal tasks; feed the agent text grids, not images.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi, Oh (2026) A neuropsychologically grounded evaluation of LLM cognitive abilities (NeuroCognition)
finding: Benchmark with an adapted Raven task (RAVEN images, 140 items, plus 200 generated text matrices), spatial working memory and card sorting, on 10 recent models. Models do better on text than image; humans show the opposite on Raven.
numbers: Human pilot on RAPM: text MC 0.430 and text generative 0.444 vs image 0.814. Model modality penalty significant for RAPM (p = .010). Format changes scores (MC to generative): GPT-5 0.540 to 0.605, Claude 0.560 to 0.385, Grok 4 Fast 0.690 to 0.555. Reasoning was disabled for Claude Sonnet 4 and Grok 4 Fast on RAPM because overthinking exhausted outputs.
limits: Small human pilot. Text matrices use string attributes, not shapes. Reasoning settings differ by model.
agent_relevance: Recent models still lose accuracy on image Raven and can over-think; a cap on thinking length and a forced text conversion are justified.

source: Kunda, Soulieres, Rozga, Goel (2016) Error patterns on the Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices test
finding: Builds a complete two-stage classification of every wrong answer on the SPM and a method that compares a group's errors with what a random guesser would produce. Applied to an AI model (ASTI, pixel-based affine and set transformations) and to autistic and typical children and adults.
numbers: Coder agreement 82% before and 95% (stage 1) / 98% (stage 2) after negotiation. Typical adults made about 7 points fewer repetition errors than random guessing; autistic adults made more repetition errors than typical adults; for children the deviation from chance was about 2%.
limits: Group differences were small. Groups differed in IQ and, for children, in SPM score, a confound the authors flag.
agent_relevance: Error type is a diagnostic signal. Logging which wrong answer the agent picks (repetition of a neighbour cell, wrong principle, incomplete correlate) shows which rule step failed.

source: Kunda et al. (2016) review of the Raven error literature
finding: Older studies (Halstead 1943, Bromley 1953, Vodegel Matzen 1994, Babcock 2002) agree that low scorers make mostly repetition errors, and middle and high scorers mostly incomplete-correlate errors. Strategy differences were noted from Binet on; the total score hides them.
numbers: Reported patterns: incomplete-correlate errors above 50% of errors in average and above-average ability samples; repetition errors above 75% of errors in some low-ability samples. Inter-rater agreement about 72% in one older coding study.
limits: Heterogeneous samples and coding schemes; summary relies on the review's reading of each study.
agent_relevance: Low ability looks like copying a neighbouring cell. A weak agent run should show the same, a cheap check that no rule was induced.

source: Kunda et al. (2016)
finding: Computational models of Raven fall in groups: rule storage and goal maintenance in working memory (Carpenter), analogy construction (Lovett, Forbus, Usher 2010), Bayesian rule induction (Little, Lewandowsky, Griffiths 2012), and visual-imagery models (ASTI). Earlier models assumed symbolic input.
numbers: ASTI uses constructive matching on pixel images and makes many repetition errors because it builds the answer from cells next to the blank.
limits: Review of models; none re-run here.
agent_relevance: Models agree on constructive matching as the human-like route. The S0 gate can check that the agent built an answer before it looked at options.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Griffiths (2012) A Bayesian model of rule induction in Raven's progressive matrices
finding: Treats rule induction as Bayesian inference: a posterior over rules given the observed cell features and a prior over rules. Fitted to correct and incorrect response choices on the Standard and Advanced matrices.
numbers: Not read: only a search-result abstract was available this session.
limits: The PDF link returned HTML; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: A posterior over a rule set suggests keeping several candidate rules alive and scoring each, rather than committing early.

source: Woodcock-Johnson Concept Formation and Analysis-Synthesis (gap note)
finding: No source on the Woodcock-Johnson Concept Formation and Analysis-Synthesis subtests was opened in this search. Angle A covered the Raven line only.
numbers: None.
limits: Gap: needs a separate fetch of the Woodcock and Mather manuals and factor loadings.
agent_relevance: Concept Formation (rule discovery from feedback) is the closer analogue to the S0 gate; needs follow-up.
